content:
Following up on #41339, which @Jon Eugster marked awaiting-zulip

#41339 to #41344 add SparsePoly R, a computable polynomial type the kernel can evaluate, together with a CommRing instance and an AlgEquiv to Polynomial R. The design is Mario's, building on a prototype of James Davenport, and goes back to a 2024 trimester in Bonn.

My original plan was to PR just this API but I added the kernel tactics in #41345 and #41346 afterwards since I was told an API on its own probably wouldn't get in. There, poly_decide proves equalities of polynomials over ℤ, poly_eval proves Polynomial.eval a p = v, and poly_dvd proves p ∣ q by long division, all without native_decide. They only work over rings whose arithmetic the kernel can evaluate, so ℤ yes, ℝ no. #41347poly_dvd_cert is independent of all this.

I also realise this overlaps to some extent with other things, like the polynomial tactic and sparse polys in Hex, though I can't really judge how much. So I guess the questions are:

1) Do we want a computable polynomial API in-tree at all?
2) And do the kernel tactics add anything that isn't already covered or better done at the meta level?

Happy to adapt, trim or close the stack depending on what people think
Thanks for starting this thread! It probably makes sense to start with also getting @Jovan Gerbscheid 's thoughts shared here

The introduced SparsePoly serves two purposes:

  1. Kernel computations: This allows us to make various polynomial tactics like poly_decide, poly_dvd and poly_eval. However, these won't work for Rat or Real because the kernel can't run their operations. So, I think we should instead strive to implement these tactics in a way that does support all types. The recently added matrix tactics (e.g. for computing the rank or determinant) follow this pattern.

  2. Direct polynomial computations: I think this can be useful for metaprogramming, but I think we should first have an explicit use case. Keep in mind that mathlib is a mathematics library, not a computer algebra library. This means that mathlib is more interested in tactics that do computations, than in the computations themselves. I made a similar point against the inclusion of dense matrices in mathlib in #mathlib4 > PR proposal: DenseMatrix for computational linear algebra.

I think it would have been better to discuss these issues on Zulip before making the PRs, since many other people have thought about this.
Thanks Jovan. For context, this came out of the Lean/LMFDB workshop. @Bhavik Mehta @Andrew Yang @David Ang we talked about this there, do you have a concrete use case in mind?
Prove irreducibility of polynomials, or factorise polynomials? Back in June/July we didn’t have Hex or any other plans for computer algebra systems, so Michail proposed his PRs directly to mathlib.
